analysis.one_liner: Makes social media verify users' ages, require parental consent for teens, and shut off algorithmic feeds for minors.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from April 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025, despite 11 senators from both parties backing it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require social media platforms to verify the age of account holders using steps beyond simply asking users to state their age. It would bar children under 13 from having accounts, require a parent or guardian's affirmative consent for users under 18, and let parents revoke that consent, which would shut the account down. It would also stop platforms from feeding teens personalized algorithmic recommendations or targeted ads. A voluntary, free digital ID program run by the Commerce Department would give people a private way to prove their age, and the FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the rules with civil penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers. Kids under 13 could be kept off social media entirely, teens under 18 would need a parent's consent and would stop receiving engagement-maximizing algorithmic feeds and targeted ads, and parents could shut down a teen's account at any time. The bill also bars platforms from using or keeping the information collected during age verification for any other purpose, which limits how the new data could be monetized.

how_it_helps.text: Platforms must verify the age of account holders using steps beyond mere self-reported age, and cannot let anyone create or keep an account whose age is unverified after two years.
Children under 13 may not use social media platforms beyond viewing content while logged out.

Platforms must get affirmative parental or guardian consent to create an account for a minor between 13 and 17, must let the parent revoke consent, and must suspend or delete the account when consent is revoked.

Platforms may not use a user's personal data in an algorithmic recommendation system, including targeted advertising, unless the user is verified as 18 or older; teens would see content ranked by context rather than by their personal data.

Information collected during age verification and parental consent cannot be used or retained for any other purpose, and the bill explicitly does not require anyone to hand over government-issued ID to a platform.

The Commerce Department would run a voluntary, no-cost pilot program for a secure digital ID that people could use to prove their age or a parental relationship without sharing underlying documents, with strict limits on record-keeping and a sunset date.
The FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the rules, with civil penalties calculated per day of violation or per user harmed.

analysis.who_pays: Social media platforms bear the direct cost: building age-verification and parental-consent systems, losing the algorithmic engagement and targeted-ad revenue they get from users under 18, and facing civil penalties for violations. Users also pay a privacy price: every account holder would have to prove their age through some identity check, which in practice means handing over documents or identity data to platforms or verification vendors.

drawbacks.text: Age verification 'beyond merely requiring attestation' for every account holder means tens of millions of Americans would have to prove their age with documents or third-party identity checks, creating a large store of sensitive identity data that did not exist before and would be a target for breaches.

The bill would have taken effect only one year after enactment, and existing accounts older than 90 days would not need age verification until two years after enactment, so full compliance was years away.

Teens under 18 would lose personalized feeds entirely, including discovery of content and communities some teens rely on for support; the bill permits only context-based suggestions not based on personal data.
Compliance costs fall on platforms of every size, and smaller platforms are less able to absorb them than the largest companies.

Privacy and civil liberties groups have argued that mandatory age verification and a government digital ID program, even a voluntary one, create surveillance and free-speech risks; the bill's answer was strict data-use limits, an explicit no-government-ID mandate for platforms, and a pilot program sunset, but the underlying tradeoff remains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefits are real and targeted: taking young teens off platforms, giving parents control, and ending engagement-optimized feeds for minors addresses concerns about social media's effects on adolescent mental health. The costs are also real: universal age verification means everyone, not just teens, must prove their identity to use social media, and that data creates a new breach and surveillance risk the bill could limit but not eliminate. The design shows its authors took the privacy objection seriously (no government ID requirement, strict data-retention limits, a voluntary pilot with a sunset), but this is a genuine tradeoff, not a free win.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2023 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held a hearing, marked it up, or voted on it in the 20 months before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the bill with Sens. Tom Cotton, Chris Murphy, and Katie Britt, an unusual four-way split of two Democrats and two Republicans.
Ten more senators, five from each party, signed on as cosponsors.

The bill's only action after introduction was being read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; the action history shows nothing further through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.
No committee hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and no version of the bill was taken up by the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social media platforms are better off, because they keep the engagement and ad revenue from teen users and face no age-verification mandate; children and teens are left without the protections the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Social media platforms kept the status quo

for.name: Sens. Tom Cotton, Chris Murphy, and Katie Britt
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction, giving it two Republicans and two Democrats from day one.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total Senate backing to 11 members.

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote, for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: NetChoice (tech industry trade group)

against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory age-verification and parental-consent mandates for social media, consistent with its public campaigns against similar state laws.

against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory age verification as a privacy and free-speech risk for all users.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's backers were evenly split by party: a lead team of two Democrats and two Republicans, and 10 cosponsors split 5 Republicans and 5 Democrats. No floor vote ever happened, so there is no roll-call to measure opposition.

industries.note: Platforms would have to build age-verification and parental-consent systems, keep children under 13 off, let parents delete teen accounts, and face civil penalties per day or per user harmed. Their loss is the algorithmic engagement of users under 18, the audience their ad business is built to maximize.
The bill bans using personal data to target advertising at anyone under 18, shrinking the pool of users who can be served personalized ads.

The Commerce Department is authorized to contract with private identity-verification providers for the digital ID pilot, creating a new compliance market. Their revenue depends on the verification mandate the bill imposes, which is also the burden on users.
